summary: Specifies how to use the LDP Multipoint Extensions over a Targeted LDP session, where the two session endpoints are not directly connected. The original multipoint extensions assumed direct connection.

eli5.summary: A rule that worked only for next-door neighbors is extended to friends farther away.

questions: how does mldp work over targeted ldp sessions
unicast replication vs multicast tunneling in mldp
subtitle: How multipoint MPLS label paths can run between routers that are not next-door neighbors.

tldr.problem: The multipoint extensions to LDP (mLDP) assumed the two ends of an LDP session are directly connected, but LDP also allows Targeted sessions between routers that are not.
tldr.mechanism: It lets a router pick an upstream LSR that is a BGP next hop or an RSVP-TE tunnel endpoint, then sends data to remote downstream routers either by unicast replication or through a multicast tunnel with upstream-assigned labels.
tldr.outcome: mLDP can now be used across Targeted LDP sessions, with the choice of method set by provisioning. No new capabilities or messages are defined.

today: RFC 7060 is a Proposed Standard, published in November 2013, and the data lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 6388 and RFC 6389.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Label Distribution Protocol (LDP) extensions for setting up Point-to-Multipoint (P2MP) and Multipoint-to-Multipoint (MP2MP) Label Switched Paths (LSPs) are specified in RFC 6388. They are generally known as Multipoint LDP (mLDP). This document uses "Multipoint" to mean either P2MP or MP2MP.

Two LDP peers that are directly connected, for example over a layer 2 medium or as neighbors in the interior routing protocol, have a directly connected session. When they are not directly connected, the session is a Targeted LDP session. The mLDP base specification does not explicitly cover Targeted sessions, and this RFC supplies that missing specification.
sections.eli5: Some friends live next door and some live across town. The old rules only covered the next-door ones, so this paper adds the rules for the ones across town.

sections.title: Choosing the Upstream LSR
sections.content:
An MP-LSP is identified by a pair <root, opaque value>: the IP address of the root node and an identifier unique in the context of that root. When router D sets up the MP-LSP <R, X>, it must find its upstream LSR, U. In RFC 6388 that is the next hop toward R, tacitly an IGP next hop, so D and U share a direct LDP session.

This RFC widens the idea in two cases. First, U may be the BGP next hop on D's path to R, with a Targeted LDP session between U and D. Second, if D's next-hop interface toward R is an RSVP-TE P2P tunnel whose remote endpoint is U, an RSVP-TE P2P tunnel is known to run from U to D, and a Targeted LDP session exists between them, D may select U. This is useful when D and U sit in an area fully meshed by RSVP-TE P2P tunnels.

The method is chosen by the Service Provider and must be made known beforehand, by provisioning, to all LSRs involved. Other methods MAY be used, but they are outside the scope of this document.
sections.eli5: Each router has to know which router is 'above' it in the tree so it can ask for the data. Now that router can be farther away than a neighbor, as long as everyone was told the rule ahead of time.

sections.title: Two Ways to Reach Remote Downstream Routers
sections.content:
With Targeted mLDP, U can have downstream neighbors D1 through Dn that it is not directly connected to. The RFC covers two ways to get a packet to them. In unicast replication, U makes n copies and unicasts each to exactly one of them. In multicast tunneling, U becomes the root of a multicast tunnel whose leaves are D1 through Dn, and sends one copy into the tunnel.

Tunneling may carry the traffic of several MP-LSPs through one tunnel. Not every leaf is on every MP-LSP, so some leaves discard packets they do not need. In the RFC's example, <R1,X1> has downstream LSRs D1 and D2, <R2,X2> has D2 and D3, and one tunnel reaches D1, D2 and D3.

Targeted mLDP MUST NOT be used unless D implements a procedure that can select a Targeted mLDP peer as its upstream LSR. When that holds, whether to use it, which of the two methods to use, and which tunnel type to use are decided by provisioning or other methods outside this specification. All nodes are presupposed to know this a priori.
sections.eli5: To give the same note to three friends far away, you can write three copies and deliver each, or you can post one copy on a bus that stops at all three houses.

sections.title: LDP Capabilities
sections.content:
Any LSR that sets up an MP-LSP must support the procedures of RFC 5561 and send and receive the P2MP Capability and/or the MP2MP Capability. This specification defines no new capabilities. Advertising those capabilities on a Targeted LDP session means the advertiser can follow the procedures in this document.

Some procedures here need upstream-assigned labels from RFC 6389. To use them with Targeted mLDP, an LSR must advertise the LDP Upstream-Assigned Label Capability on the Targeted LDP session.
sections.eli5: Before playing, each side says what games it knows. Saying you know the multipoint game over a long-distance link means you know these new rules too.

sections.title: Unicast Replication
sections.content:
With unicast replication the mLDP procedures are exactly those of RFC 6388, except that the upstream LSR is chosen as above and is not necessarily the IGP next hop. Say D1 and D2 both set up the P2MP MP-LSP <R,X> with U upstream. Each binds a label (L1 and L2) and tells U in a Label Mapping message. D1 and D2 do not coordinate, so L1 and L2 may be equal or different. To send a packet, U copies it, pushes L1 and unicasts it to D1, then copies it again, pushes L2 and unicasts it to D2.

It also works for MP2MP LSPs. If U assigned L3 for traffic received from D1 and L4 for traffic from D2, a packet arriving with L3 on top came from D1, so U swaps L3 for L2 and unicasts a copy to D2 and does not send one back to D1. All labels here are downstream-assigned.

How the unicast is done is a local matter. If it uses MPLS, U must push another label on each copy to reach D1 or D2, and penultimate-hop popping for that label is legitimate.
sections.eli5: You write a separate letter to each friend and put their own name on it. The friend who sent you something does not get a copy of their own message back.

sections.title: Multicast Tunneling
sections.content:
With a multicast tunnel, U need not send one copy per receiver, because replication happens downstream in the tunnel. So the label bound to the MP-LSP must be an upstream-assigned label chosen by U. This changes the RFC 6388 procedure: D1 and D2 send Label Request messages to U (following Section 4 of RFC 6389) instead of Label Mapping messages. U replies with a Label Mapping message carrying upstream-assigned label L and an Interface TLV that identifies the multicast tunnel. When U sends a packet it pushes L and then the tunnel's own label.

If L is 3, Implicit NULL, the tunnel carries only that one MP-LSP and no upstream-assigned label is pushed. The tunnel type is set by provisioning, and RFC 6389 has encodings for an mLDP MP-LSP, an RSVP-TE P2MP LSP and other types. Tunneling MP2MP LSPs through P2MP or MP2MP LSPs is out of scope.

If the tunnel is an mLDP MP-LSP or RSVP-TE P2MP LSP, L is the second label in the stack, and penultimate-hop popping MUST NOT be done, because the top label gives the context for reading the second (see RFC 5331). U MAY put several MP-LSPs in one tunnel but MUST give each a distinct upstream-assigned label so packets can be demultiplexed. In the earlier example D3 gets <R1,X1> packets but does not recognize their label and discards them. D must stay joined to the tunnel as long as U is its upstream LSR for any MP-LSP on it. The RFC sets no rules for when to aggregate MP-LSPs.
sections.eli5: Instead of mailing each friend a copy, you put one copy on a shared bus with a numbered ticket on it. Each friend only reads notes with the ticket numbers they asked about and throws away the rest.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says it raises no new security considerations beyond those discussed in the LDP specification (RFC 5036), RFC 6389 and RFC 5331.
sections.eli5: Nothing new here is risky. The safety rules of the older documents still apply.
